faq.q: How does a syringe suck up liquid?
faq.a: Pulling the plunger lowers the pressure inside the barrel. The higher air pressure on the liquid outside then pushes it into the syringe.

faq.q: Why does liquid come out when you push the plunger?
faq.a: Pushing shrinks the space inside the barrel and raises the pressure, so the liquid is forced out through the only opening, the tip.
asks: What pushes liquid out of a syringe?

faq.q: Why is it hard to pull a plunger when the end is blocked?
faq.a: Pulling makes a low-pressure space inside with nothing to fill it, so the air outside pushes hard on the plunger, trying to push it back in.
asks: Why does a blocked syringe spring back?

faq.q: Why do nurses flick a syringe?
faq.a: Flicking makes air bubbles rise to the top so they can be pushed out before an injection, because air should not be injected.
asks: Why get air out of a syringe?

faq.q: Where else is the syringe idea used?
faq.a: The same idea appears in pipettes, water pistols, bicycle pumps and the master cylinder of a car brake.

facts: A syringe fills because outside air pressure pushes liquid into the low-pressure space made by pulling the plunger.
Liquids barely squash, so pushing a plunger sends the liquid out of the syringe tip.
